subject: Accounting
title: Variance Analysis
description: Learn Variance Analysis in one minute.

hook.text: You budgeted $100,000 for materials but spent $115,000. Why? Variance analysis finds out.

buildup.text: Variance is the difference between budgeted and actual results. It can be favorable or unfavorable.

discovery.text: Breaking it down reveals whether the issue was price (paid too much) or quantity (used too much).

twist.text: A favorable variance isn't always good—buying cheap materials might lead to costly defects later.

climax.text: Managers investigate significant variances and take corrective action before small gaps become big ones.

punchline.text: Variances ask: what went wrong, and why?

quiz.question: What does variance analysis compare?
options: This year's revenue to last year's

details.summary: Variance analysis compares actual results to budgeted amounts and breaks the differences into meaningful components—price variances and quantity variances—so managers can identify exactly where and why performance deviated from plan.
details.whyItMatters: Knowing profit was off by $50,000 isn't actionable. Knowing that $30,000 came from higher material prices and $20,000 from excess usage gives managers specific problems to solve.
takeaways: A variance is favorable when actual results are better than budgeted, unfavorable when worse
Price variances measure the impact of paying more or less than expected per unit of input
Quantity variances measure the impact of using more or less input than the standard allows

faq.question: What is variance analysis?
faq.answer: Variance analysis is the process of comparing actual costs and revenues to their budgeted amounts, then decomposing the differences into specific causes. It separates the impact of price changes from the impact of quantity changes to identify actionable issues.

faq.question: What is the difference between a price variance and a quantity variance?
faq.answer: A price variance measures the financial impact of paying a different price than budgeted for inputs (materials, labor). A quantity variance measures the impact of using a different amount of input than the standard. Together they explain the total spending variance.
